title: Quantum circuit compilation with constant overhead
authors: Chenyi Zhang, Xinyu Tan, Robin Kothari, David Gosset, Craig Gidney
abstract: Compiling a continuous gate set to a discrete universal gate set generally incurs an overhead. A circuit composed of $G$ arbitrary one- and two-qubit gates can be $ε$-approximated by a sequence of gates from $\{H,T,\mathrm{CNOT}\}$ by replacing each original gate by a sequence of $O(\log(G/ε))$ elementary gates. We show that this overhead can be avoided using adaptivity for polynomial-sized circuits with inverse-polynomial target error, which is optimal.
summary: This paper presents a breakthrough in quantum circuit compilation, demonstrating a method to compile circuits from continuous gate sets to discrete universal gates with only constant overhead. By leveraging adaptivity and sophisticated quantum gadgets, the authors achieve gate counts that scale linearly with the original circuit size, which is crucial for practical quantum computation.
main_problem: The paper addresses the overhead incurred when compiling quantum circuits defined by an arbitrary continuous gate set down to a discrete universal gate set, such as {H, T, CNOT}.
main_result: They show that by employing adaptivity for polynomial-sized circuits with inverse-polynomial target error, the compilation overhead can be reduced to a constant factor, achieving $O(G)$ gate complexity.
method: The authors utilize advanced techniques including adaptive circuit design, state injection and phase-halving gadgets, and encoding tricks to manage the required precision and gate count.
model_or_system: The model is quantum circuits composed of one- and two-qubit gates, which are approximated using the discrete gate set {H, T, CNOT}. Key components include the phase gradient state and various quantum gadgets.
key_observables: Gate count, circuit depth, and the achievable target error $\epsilon$.
important_parameters: The number of gates $G$, the target error $\epsilon$, and the circuit size $n$ (related to $G$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the optimal preparation of the phase gradient state and the successful implementation of complex subroutines like the SELECT function.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the State Injection and Phase-Halving gadgets, and the structure of the tree data used for the SELECT function implementation.
paper_structure: The paper builds from general compilation overhead reduction (Theorem 1) to specific circuit implementations (Theorem 2), detailing the preparation of resource states (Theorem 3), and finally implementing complex functions like phase-halving and SELECT.
why_interesting: This work provides fundamental theoretical advances in quantum compilation, directly impacting the feasibility and resource estimation for implementing complex quantum algorithms on near-term hardware.
